LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds

Pengcheng Zhou1,†\dagger, Xuanyu Liu2,†\dagger, Yanchen Yin3, Tianjie Ju1, Bobo Li1,
Shengqiong Wu4,*, Hao Fei4, Mong-Li Lee1, Wynne Hsu1

1National University of Singapore, 2Zhejiang University,
3Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, 4University of Oxford

\tl_set:Ne\linkbadge

linkbadge \linkbadge  Project Page   \linkbadge  GeoWorld Code   \linkbadge  LiveGeo Benchmark

We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

1 Introduction

Geographic intelligence, the ability to understand, reason about, and act upon real-world geographic information, has advanced substantially with the emergence of large language and vision-language models (Roberts et al., 2023; Manvi et al., 2024; Dihan et al., 2025) and is increasingly being deployed in diverse practical applications (Ju et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2024). In parallel, its evaluation has evolved considerably. Early benchmarks primarily assessed isolated capabilities, such as geographic knowledge and spatial reasoning (Roberts et al., 2023; Manvi et al., 2024), or perception-oriented abilities including image geolocation and map reasoning (Dihan et al., 2025). These tasks typically operate over fixed inputs and do not require interaction with an external environment. With the emergence of agentic systems, evaluation has shifted toward end-to-end task execution in geographic environments. Recent benchmarks place agents in simulated or real-world urban settings (Feng et al., 2025b; Lai et al., 2026), or formulate realistic planning scenarios in which agents must actively acquire information, interact with external tools, and construct feasible plans (Xie et al., 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026a; Cheng et al., 2026b; Song et al., 2026). Collectively, these efforts have broadened both the geographic information agents must process and the complexity of the tasks they must accomplish.

However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate agents in environments where the task-relevant geographic state remains fixed during execution, typically using a static snapshot of the world (Cheng et al., 2026a; Song et al., 2026). Even benchmarks that incorporate environmental dynamics generally focus on specific urban processes or predefined disruptions that are explicitly exposed to the agent (Feng et al., 2025b; Lai et al., 2026; Karmakar et al., 2026). Real-world geographic environments, by contrast, evolve continuously and independently of the agent, such as road conditions, place availability, and regional events, while only some of these changes matter to the task. Reliable decision-making in such circumstances therefore requires agents not only to act on available and dynamic information, but also to acquire task-relevant evidence, verify whether prior evidence and assumptions remain valid, and revise decisions when they do not. A separate limitation concerns what existing benchmarks evaluate (Table 1). Because they typically focus on specific applications or workflows, they primarily measure whether an end task can be completed rather than which geographic constraints and decision dependencies the agent understands and relies on. Consequently, failures are difficult to attribute to deficiencies in geographic understanding, feasibility assessment, or the ability to maintain valid decisions over time. This raises a central question: can agents sustain reliable decision-making in continuously evolving geographic environments while keeping their decisions grounded in evidence that remains valid as the world changes?

To address this question, we first develop GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving interactive environment platform grounded in real-world urban geography. GeoWorld jointly maintains multiple world states, including road networks, place states, and regional events, and allows external events to unfold according to their own temporal processes, independent of agent actions. The platform enables different tasks to be executed within a unified and continuously evolving geographic world while preserving verifiable world states throughout. Building on GeoWorld, we further introduce LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating the reliable geographic decision-making of general-purpose LLM agents in continuously evolving environments. LiveGeo contains 7 task categories and 1,237 verifiable task instances, covering 6 real-world cities, 1,376 POIs, and 31 tool types, with matched static and dynamic task settings. Rather than making decisions based only on the environmental state at a single point in time, agents in LiveGeo must actively acquire relevant information during task execution and adjust their plans when changes in the world state invalidate the basis of previous decisions.

We systematically evaluate 9 representative proprietary and open-source models under a unified ReAct-based agent scaffold and tool-access protocol. Our results show that current agents remain far from solving geographic decision-making even on atomic tasks: on extensively studied tasks such as place grounding and place discovery, the strongest agent achieves only 38.0% pass@1. Performance drops further on compositional tasks, indicating that the primary difficulty lies not merely in invoking individual tools, but in jointly satisfying multiple interdependent geographic constraints. World dynamics introduce an additional and consistent performance cost: under matched dynamic settings, performance decreases by 70.3% under Task-Only Dynamics and 79.3% under Shared Dynamics relative to the corresponding static settings across models and task categories. Further analysis identifies Evidence Hallucination in static settings and Change Monitoring Failure in dynamic settings as major bottlenecks to reliable decision-making. Agents often make unsupported geographic claims and fail to acquire updated information after necessary world changes. These results show that current agents have some ability to make one-shot decisions, but remain limited in maintaining decision validity as the world continues to evolve.

Our main contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic platform grounded in real-world urban structure, in which world states evolve independently of agent actions while remaining fully verifiable over time.

  • •

    We present LiveGeo, a capability-structured benchmark with matched static and dynamic settings for evaluating general-purpose LLM agents on continuous information acquisition, evidence validation, and adaptive replanning in evolving geographic environments.

  • •

    We conduct a systematic evaluation of representative LLM agents on LiveGeo, revealing substantial performance degradation under world dynamics and characterizing key failure modes in maintaining evidence-grounded decisions and adapting plans as the environment changes.

2 Related Work

Geographic Intelligence Benchmarks Existing geographic intelligence benchmarks cover a broad range of capabilities, from geographic knowledge and spatial reasoning to visual geographic understanding and real-world decision-making. One line of work examines the geographic knowledge encoded in language models and their ability to reason about spatial relations (Roberts et al., 2023; Manvi et al., 2024); MapEval further evaluates reasoning over maps and other structured geographic representations (Dihan et al., 2025). Another line of work focuses on visual geographic understanding. Visual geolocation benchmarks evaluate whether models can infer real-world locations from geographic cues in street-level and cross-view imagery (Astruc et al., 2024; Kristoffersen et al., 2026; Talreja et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026); remote-sensing and geospatial vision-language benchmarks further cover visual question answering, scene and object understanding, visual grounding, and spatial and relational reasoning (Kuckreja et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Danish et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). A separate line of work extends geographic intelligence evaluation to interactive decision-making. CityBench (Feng et al., 2025b) and USTBench (Lai et al., 2026) place agents in urban environments and evaluate their ability to interpret and use heterogeneous urban information; benchmarks for travel, mobility, and local-life planning further require agents to actively acquire information, invoke external tools, and construct feasible plans under real-world constraints (Xie et al., 2024; Chaudhuri et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026a; Cheng et al., 2026b; Song et al., 2026). These studies cover diverse input modalities and application settings, but their task structures typically focus on specific problems or application workflows. LiveGeo instead adopts a capability-structured evaluation perspective, progressing from basic geographic operations to compositional decisions whose feasibility is jointly determined by multiple interdependent constraints.

Interactive and Dynamic Geographic Environments Interactive urban environments have been used to evaluate agents’ reasoning and decision-making over complex spatiotemporal states. Existing urban-agent benchmarks simulate urban processes or provide interactive environments in which agents can plan and adapt as spatiotemporal conditions evolve (Feng et al., 2025b; Lai et al., 2026); more recent work has also begun to evaluate adaptation to real-world disruptions, such as revising existing travel plans when transportation or place availability changes (Karmakar et al., 2026). However, existing dynamic evaluations are typically organized around specific urban processes or application tasks, and less often systematically assess whether the evidence supporting a decision remains valid as the environment changes, and whether the decision should be updated accordingly. This aspect is also difficult to capture in some real-world planning benchmarks, where external tool outputs are stabilized through caching or deterministic replay, leaving the information available during task execution unchanged (Cheng et al., 2026a; Song et al., 2026). LiveGeo places this problem within a unified geographic world, GeoWorld, where changes in external states can alter the evidence on which an ongoing geographic task depends; whether a change affects the current decision is determined jointly by the task and the world state. Accordingly, LiveGeo focuses not on whether an agent can respond to a single predefined disruption, but on whether it can maintain consistency between evidence and decisions in a continuously evolving geographic environment.

3 GeoWorld

GeoWorld provides a persistent geographic environment in which heterogeneous world states are grounded in a shared spatial structure and evolve along a common timeline. Its architecture comprises three interconnected components: world state representation, temporal world dynamics, and an agent-world interface, as illustrated in Figure 2.

World State Representation

GeoWorld represents the geographic world at time tt as Wt=(G,Xt)W_{t}=(G,X_{t}), where GG captures the relatively stable geographic structure, including places, roads, regions, and their spatial relations, while XtX_{t} describes dynamic conditions such as traffic, weather, place status, and regional events. Rather than maintaining these states as independent data sources, GeoWorld associates them with a common set of geographic entities and spatial references, providing a consistent spatial foundation for world-state updates and agent observations. We construct the geographic environment from real-world data, primarily using Google Places, geocoding, and routing services (Google Maps Platform, 2026). The current implementation spans six cities: Shanghai, Tokyo, Singapore, London, New York, and Cape Town, comprising 88 regions, 1,376 POIs, and 107,372 cached route records. Details of the geographic representation, data preprocessing, and spatial coverage are provided in Appendix A.1.

Temporal World Dynamics.

Building on this shared spatial representation, GeoWorld models how geographic conditions change over time. A global virtual clock provides a common temporal reference for heterogeneous state updates, each defined by an effective time and, where applicable, a duration. Each episode begins at a specified time and advances within a bounded temporal window. As the clock advances, GeoWorld resolves scheduled changes to determine the world state WtW_{t} at the current time. These changes are exogenous to agent actions, ensuring that the underlying world evolves according to a predefined trajectory rather than being altered by agent decisions. This separation enables reproducible and replayable world dynamics while allowing agents to encounter changing conditions during task execution. Further details of clock management and temporal state updates are provided in Appendix A.2.

Agent-World Interface.

To expose the evolving world to agents, GeoWorld provides a unified tool interface for place search, routing and traffic, weather, place status, and regional events. All tool responses are resolved against the world state at the current virtual time, ensuring that agents observe temporally and spatially consistent information across different services. GeoWorld records agent queries, tool observations, and actions together with their corresponding timestamps and world-state references. These aligned interaction traces capture both the information available to agents and their subsequent decisions, providing a basis for reconstructing task execution and evaluating agent behavior under evolving world conditions. The complete tool set and interaction protocol are described in Appendix A.3.

4 LiveGeo

Building on GeoWorld, LiveGeo provides a benchmark for evaluating geographic decision-making under both static and evolving world conditions. It organizes tasks by the geographic capabilities they require and uses matched static-dynamic settings to examine whether agents can not only make valid initial decisions but also reassess and revise them as the underlying world changes.

4.1 Task Taxonomy

As summarized in Table 2, LiveGeo organizes tasks along two dimensions: geographic capability and temporal setting.

Geographic Capabilities.

We consider seven task categories, comprising three atomic and four compositional tasks. Atomic Geo Tasks target fundamental geographic operations: Grounding identifies and localizes geographic entities; Discovery selects places satisfying spatial, semantic, or situational constraints; and Mobility Planning constructs feasible routes or travel plans under transportation constraints.

Compositional Geo Tasks integrate these operations into more complex decision scenarios, emphasizing different forms of interdependence. Multi-Entity tasks coordinate constraints across multiple participants, places, or activities; Long-Horizon tasks involve sequences of interdependent decisions; Safety-Aware tasks require decisions to account for environmental or situational risks; and Region-Aware tasks incorporate region-specific geographic structures and constraints. These tasks extend beyond individual geographic operations to evaluate whether multiple decisions and their associated constraints can be satisfied jointly.

Temporal Settings.

To examine decision-making under changing conditions, LiveGeo instantiates selected tasks in matched static and dynamic settings. In the static setting, the relevant world state remains fixed throughout task execution. In the dynamic setting, task-relevant conditions, including traffic, weather, place status, and availability, may change over time. Each matched pair shares the same initial world state, task constraints, and user request, differing in the introduction of temporal state changes. This design allows us to examine how agents respond when previously valid decisions must be reassessed or revised, while controlling for the initial task requirements. Complete task definitions and examples are provided in Appendix B.1.

4.2 Benchmark Construction

Construction Pipeline.

Following the task taxonomy, LiveGeo first constructs verified static tasks and then introduces controlled world changes to create matched dynamic counterparts. This process preserves the initial task requirements while enabling evaluation under evolving conditions, as illustrated in Figure 3.

(a) Static task construction. Given an initial world state W0=(G,X0)W_{0}=(G,X_{0}), we first identify a feasible reference solution G​T0GT_{0} and derive a set of constraints C0C_{0} from the corresponding geographic facts. For example, in the group-dinner scenario in Figure 3, Restaurant A is selected as a reference solution, with constraints requiring vegetarian options, availability at the requested dinner time, and travel times within 20 minutes for all participants. We then apply programmatic checks and constraint solvers to verify that the reference solution satisfies all constraints, that the constraints are grounded in the world state, and that the information required to solve the task is accessible through the agent’s tools. Once verified, an LLM converts the structured task into a natural-language user request while preserving its requirements and withholding the reference solution. The request is subsequently reviewed by human annotators, and only approved tasks are retained.

(b) Dynamic task construction. For each selected static task, we construct a dynamic counterpart preserving the initial world state W0W_{0}, constraints C0C_{0}, reference solution G​T0GT_{0}, and user request. We then specify an updated reference solution G​T1GT_{1} and use an LLM to propose a sequence of timestamped events that affect the world state. In the group-dinner example, Restaurant A becomes unavailable while Restaurant B extends its opening hours, requiring the original choice to be reconsidered. Each event specifies an observable description and a corresponding world-state update. We verify the temporal consistency of the event sequence, the validity of the reference solutions under their corresponding world states, and the observability of task-relevant changes through the agent’s tools. The events are reviewed by human annotators before inclusion in the benchmark. Consequently, matched tasks begin with the same decision problem but differ in the evolution of the underlying world, allowing us to evaluate whether agents can maintain valid decisions as conditions change.

Benchmark Statistics.

LiveGeo contains 1,237 task instances across seven geographic task categories, including 1,088 static and 149 matched dynamic instances. Spanning six cities, the benchmark covers diverse geographic scenarios, including place discovery across different POI categories, mobility planning with multiple transportation modes, and compositional decisions involving multiple participants or multi-day itineraries. Detailed task distributions and geographic coverage are reported in Appendix B.4, while reference-solution selection, constraint generation, and verification procedures are described in Appendix B.2.

4.3 Evaluation Protocol

LiveGeo evaluates agents through the unified GeoWorld interface, using the same tool access and interaction protocol across tasks. Static tasks are executed against a fixed world state, whereas dynamic tasks unfold within a bounded virtual-time window following a predefined event sequence. Agents decide when to query the environment, advance virtual time, and revisit earlier decisions. Their interactions are recorded alongside the corresponding world states, enabling both outcome-based verification and trajectory-level analysis.

We determine task success using task-specific verification criteria. These criteria cover four main aspects of geographic decision-making, with the applicable aspects varying across task categories. Decision Correctness checks whether the final decision meets the task-specific correctness criteria, including place selection and feasibility judgments. Plan Executability further checks whether the generated decisions satisfy the relevant spatial, temporal, transportation mode, and other operational constraints. Beyond outcome validity, Evidence Support assesses whether the agent’s interaction history contains observations that substantiate its decisions. For dynamic tasks, Dynamic Adaptability further examines whether agents respond to task-relevant world changes by revalidating and, when necessary, revising their decisions.

Evaluation relies on predefined output contracts and task-specific constraint checks. State-aligned interaction traces further support evidence verification and analysis of agent behavior under changing conditions. Detailed metrics, verification rules, and trajectory analysis procedures are provided in Appendix B.3.

5 Experiment

Our analysis proceeds in three steps, from forming decisions, to maintaining them as the world evolves, to locating where reliability breaks down:

  • •

    Q1: How well can current agents make valid geographic decisions? (Section 5.2)

  • •

    Q2: How well can current agents maintain valid geographic decisions as the world evolves? (Sections 5.3 and 5.4)

  • •

    Q3: Where does reliable decision-making break down? (Section 5.5)

Additional task-specific analyses are provided in Appendix C.3.

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate representative proprietary and open-source models (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; Google DeepMind, 2026; SpaceXAI, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026; Team et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026) under a unified ReAct-based agent scaffold. All models receive the same tool-access protocol and interaction budget, with a maximum of 200 interaction steps per task. Task-specific output contracts are used to standardize the required response format for different task categories, while remaining identical across models evaluated on the same task. We retain the full interaction context throughout execution, with all evaluated models supporting context windows of at least 128K tokens. The temperature is set to 0.1, with a maximum generation length of 10K tokens per turn. For dynamic tasks, all models are evaluated against the same replayed world timeline and event schedule, ensuring that each model encounters identical environmental changes. Each task instance is evaluated over three independent runs. Detailed model versions, prompts, output contracts, and runtime configurations are provided in Appendix C.1.

5.2 Geographic Decision-Making Performance

Table 3 presents the performance of nine models across seven static geographic decision-making task categories. Overall, current agents remain limited in their geographic decision-making capabilities, with even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.7 Flash, achieving an overall success rate of only 27.8%. Meanwhile, models exhibit distinct capability profiles across tasks. For example, Gemini 3.7 Flash achieves 37.1% and 38.0% on Grounding and Discovery, respectively, but only 19.4% on Mobility Planning, compared with 31.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Qwen3.8-Max performs best on Multi-Entity at 43.8%, while Claude Sonnet 5 leads Safety-Aware at 19.8%.

Task-level results further reveal substantial differences in the difficulty of geographic decisions. Grounding, Discovery, and Mobility Planning achieve comparable average success rates of 23.5%, 24.1%, and 22.0%, respectively. Notably, Multi-Entity achieves the highest average success rate (30.8%), despite requiring decisions that jointly satisfy constraints across multiple participants. In contrast, Safety-Aware, another compositional task category, achieves only 12.9%. This disparity suggests that the difficulty of compositional geographic decisions depends not merely on combining multiple constraints, but also on the nature of the information and conditions required to establish decision validity. The most pronounced limitation emerges in Long-Horizon tasks, where the average success rate drops to 3.4%, and even the best-performing model reaches only 8.7%. These tasks require maintaining feasibility across interdependent decisions, where earlier choices constrain subsequent options. The sharp performance decline highlights the difficulty of producing end-to-end feasible plans, even when the underlying geographic state remains unchanged.

5.3 Impact of World Dynamics

To examine how world dynamics affect geographic decision reliability, we evaluate nine models under Static, Task-Only Dynamics, and Shared Dynamics using 149 matched tasks. As shown in Table 3, mean success drops from 19.1% under Static to 5.7% and 4.0% under Task-Only and Shared Dynamics, respectively, corresponding to relative declines of 70.3% and 79.3%. Notably, substantial degradation already occurs under Task-Only Dynamics, with a further decline under Shared Dynamics. However, the impact varies considerably across models. While Claude Sonnet 5 drops from 22.8% under Static to 2.7% and 2.0% under the two dynamic settings, Gemini 3.7 Flash retains much higher success rates, declining from 26.2% to 14.1% and 13.4%. These contrasting outcomes show that models with comparable static performance can differ substantially in their robustness to world changes. Figure 4 further illustrates that dynamic failures arise not only when agents miss updated geographic information, but also when they fail to incorporate correctly acquired updates into their final decisions. We systematically examine these behaviors in Section 5.4.

The impact of world dynamics also varies across geographic decision requirements. As shown in Figure 5, Region-Aware, Safety-Aware, and Multi-Entity experience average declines of 26.7, 16.0, and 11.1 percentage points under Task-Only Dynamics, respectively, compared with 26.0, 16.7, and 15.6 points under Shared Dynamics. In contrast, Mobility Planning shows smaller declines of 4.8 and 9.7 points, with three models even improving under Task-Only Dynamics. One possible explanation is that traffic changes may be captured through routine routing queries, whereas changes affecting regional restrictions, safety conditions, or participant constraints may require agents to identify relevant information needs across multiple constraints and reassess candidate validity. The additional degradation of Multi-Entity under Shared Dynamics further suggests that different task requirements may be affected differently by shared-world changes. Long-Horizon remains near the performance floor across all settings, limiting meaningful comparisons of additional degradation. We further examine the types of world changes affecting different task categories in Appendix C.3.8.

To further investigate how information acquisition affects dynamic decision-making, we evaluate three models under an additional Explicit Update setting, where all necessary task-related events are directly provided. As shown in Figure 6(a), providing these updates does not restore static-level performance: the three models’ mean success rate drops from 21.9% under Static to 16.3% under Explicit Update. This indicates that access to updated information alone is insufficient to ensure valid decisions under changed geographic conditions. When agents must discover the relevant updates themselves under Task-Only Dynamics, mean success drops further to 7.2%. Notably, the relative decline from Explicit Update to Task-Only Dynamics is particularly pronounced for GPT-5.6 Sol (75.0%) and Claude Opus 5 (69.6%), compared with Gemini 3.7 Flash (38.2%), suggesting substantial differences in sensitivity to information acquisition requirements. Performance declines further to 5.4% under Shared Dynamics, where task-relevant events occur alongside unrelated world changes.

To investigate the relationship between the performance declines observed above and world events, we examine how the number of necessary and unrelated events affect conditional success loss. As shown in Figure 6(c), among model–task pairs that succeed under Static, conditional success loss rises from 66.7% to 100.0% as the number of necessary events increases. This suggests that processing multiple updates makes it increasingly challenging for agents to maintain valid decisions. Similarly, Figure 6(b) shows that conditional success loss increases from 42.1% to 75.0% with the number of unrelated events, indicating that background world changes may further complicate decision maintenance. Overall, the increase in necessary events is associated with more pronounced success loss than the increase in unrelated events, as agents must not only acquire all relevant updates but also understand their implications for existing decisions and correctly incorporate multiple updates into their decision-making. We further investigate these challenges in Section 5.4.

5.4 Decision Maintenance under World Changes

To investigate why agents struggle to maintain valid decisions in evolving geographic environments, we analyze state-aligned interaction trajectories from 9 models on 149 matched tasks, with three independent runs per model-task pair, yielding 4,023 executions under each dynamic setting. We examine two aspects of decision maintenance: whether agents acquire the information needed to track relevant world changes, and whether they correctly incorporate the observed changes into their final decisions.

When do agents query?

As shown in Figure 7(a), agents concentrate most information queries in the early stage of a task, with approximately 72–95% of queries occurring in the first third of the virtual-time window. This pattern persists across both dynamic settings, despite substantial differences in query volume across models. For instance, Gemini 3.7 Flash issues nearly three times as many queries as GPT-5.6 Sol under Task-Only Dynamics (25.9 versus 8.6 per task), yet both concentrate over 80% of their queries in the early phase. Shared Dynamics also induces no systematic shift toward later querying, suggesting that agents do not substantially adapt their information-seeking behavior to the more complex event environment. Nevertheless, Figure 7(b) shows positive model-level correlations between late-phase querying and task success across both settings (r=0.61r=0.61-0.800.80). Although these correlations do not establish causality, they motivate a closer examination of whether agents revisit information affected by world changes.

Do agents track relevant changes?

Querying throughout a task does not necessarily ensure that agents observe the changes relevant to their decisions. We therefore align queries with the effective times and affected entities of necessary events. As shown in Figure 8(a), only 20.6% and 18.0% of eligible runs issue targeted queries after necessary events under Task-Only and Shared Dynamics, respectively. Moreover, among runs that had previously acquired the affected information, 31.1% and 33.6% never recheck it after the change. Figure 8(b) further shows that issuing more queries does not consistently improve necessary-event coverage: coverage remains below 30% across all total-query-count groups. In contrast, runs with at least one post-event targeted query exhibit substantially higher event coverage than those without such queries. While this association partly follows from how targeted queries and event observation are defined, it highlights the importance of reaching the information actually affected by a change, rather than simply increasing query volume.

Does observing changes lead to valid decisions?

Even when agents acquire necessary updates, they may fail to incorporate them into their final decisions. Figure 9(a) shows that only 14.1% and 11.8% of runs observe all necessary events under Task-Only and Shared Dynamics, respectively, with substantial variation across models. However, incomplete observation is only part of the problem. Among runs that observe every necessary event, Figure 9(b) shows that 76.7% and 73.9% correctly report the events, whereas only 43.1% and 39.9% produce correct final decisions. Notably, 36.4% and 38.6% correctly report the relevant changes but still reach incorrect decisions. This reveals a distinct gap between acquiring accurate information about the current geographic state and using that information to satisfy the task constraints. Thus, failures in dynamic decision maintenance arise not only from incomplete awareness of world changes, but also from difficulties in translating observed changes into valid decisions.

5.5 Failure Modes in Geographic Decision-Making

To identify where geographic decision-making breaks down, we analyze state-aligned interaction trajectories and attribute failed executions to their primary failure modes under static and dynamic settings. We employ a two-stage LLM-based attribution protocol, in which candidate causes are proposed and independently reviewed using trajectory and world-state evidence. Failure definitions, attribution procedures, and representative cases are provided in Appendices C.2 and C.4, with task-level analyses in Appendix C.3.

Failure Modes under Static Conditions.

As shown in Figure 10, static geographic decision-making failures are predominantly associated with how agents acquire, verify, and integrate geographic evidence. Evidence Hallucination is the most prevalent failure mode, accounting for 37.3% of attributed failures, followed by Intent-to-Search Failure (20.4%) and Discriminative Verification Failure (16.1%). Together with Evidence Integration Failure (8.7%), these evidence-related categories account for 82.5% of attributed failures, substantially exceeding those associated with spatial reasoning or visual perception. This suggests that producing geographically valid decisions is limited not only by spatial understanding, but also by the reliability of the evidence used to support candidate choices. Although evidence hallucination is the dominant failure mode for most models, their failure profiles differ. For instance, Claude Sonnet 5 exhibits comparable proportions of search failures (29.8%) and evidence hallucination (29.6%), whereas Gemini 3.7 Flash shows a substantial proportion of discriminative verification failures (28.2%). These variations indicate that failures can arise at different stages of evidence-based decision-making, rather than reflecting a single shared weakness across models.

Failure Modes under World Dynamics.

Under evolving geographic conditions, the failure distribution becomes strongly concentrated in Change Monitoring Failure, which accounts for 79.4% of primary attributions and is the largest failure category for every model (Figure 11). This contrasts with the more distributed failure profiles under Static, indicating that maintaining awareness of relevant world changes is a dominant challenge in dynamic decision-making. This finding is consistent with the behavioral evidence in Section 5.4, where agents concentrate queries early and infrequently revisit affected entities after changes occur. However, the dominance of monitoring failures does not imply that subsequent decision revision is reliable. Because each failed execution receives a single primary attribution, earlier monitoring failures may obscure downstream difficulties. Indeed, the decision-maintenance analysis shows that agents frequently produce incorrect decisions even after observing and correctly reporting necessary changes. Together, these results identify two distinct limitations: insufficient monitoring of an evolving geographic world and unreliable incorporation of observed changes into subsequent decisions.

6 Conclusion & Discussion

We introduced GeoWorld, a persistent geographic environment in which world states evolve through independently occurring events, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating agents’ ability to make and maintain valid geographic decisions under static and dynamic conditions. By aligning agent interactions with verifiable world states, our framework enables not only systematic evaluation of decision outcomes but also trajectory-level analysis of how agents acquire information, respond to changes, and revise decisions. Experiments across nine models reveal substantial limitations in geographic decision-making, with performance varying across decision requirements and deteriorating markedly under world dynamics. Further behavioral and failure analyses identify distinct bottlenecks: under static conditions, agents struggle to acquire, verify, and integrate geographic evidence; under dynamic conditions, they frequently fail to monitor relevant changes and may still produce invalid decisions even after observing the necessary updates.

These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between establishing decision validity and maintaining it over time. Reliable geographic agents must go beyond making decisions from a snapshot of the world: they need to track the conditions on which their decisions depend, detect when those conditions change, and reassess affected choices while preserving other applicable constraints. GeoWorld and LiveGeo provide a verifiable testbed for studying these capabilities, supporting future research toward agents that can sustain valid decisions in continuously evolving geographic environments.

Appendix

Appendix A GeoWorld: Design and Implementation Details

A.1 Geographic World Instantiation

Table 4 summarizes the geographic assets in the current GeoWorld evaluation version across six cities, including Regions, POIs, and cached route records. In GeoWorld, a Region is a functional urban area constructed around real-world locations and their associated roles. Each Region is described by its name, center coordinates, functional labels, supporting evidence, and provenance information, and is represented spatially by its center point. Candidate Regions are generated during city discovery and reviewed with reference to urban geographic structure, functional roles, and supporting map and web evidence. POIs are associated with Regions based on spatial proximity, using a maximum assignment distance of 3,500 m. This representation provides a common spatial reference for downstream POI retrieval, task constraints, and region-level events. POIs are primarily collected through the Google Places API (Google Maps Platform, 2026). GeoWorld performs Nearby Search and Text Search around Region centers, transportation corridor nodes, and corridor service areas, and uses Place Details to supplement place attributes. The search covers a predefined set of categories, such as dining, retail, accommodation, healthcare, and education. Candidate POIs are then subject to coordinate checks, city-boundary filtering, provider-identity deduplication, and quality filtering. Deduplication prioritizes provider identities such as Google place_id, thereby preventing the same location from being included multiple times across different searches. For service attributes required by downstream tasks, GeoWorld further combines Place Details with publicly available web evidence to supplement opening information, service descriptions, menus, and other verifiable merchant information. Route assets are progressively constructed around urban transportation corridors and the origin–destination pairs required by downstream tasks. Routes are obtained through the Google Routes API (Google Maps Platform, 2026), using three travel modes: DRIVE, WALK, and TRANSIT. Each cached route record contains a normalized origin and destination, travel mode, distance, estimated duration, route geometry.

GeoWorld retains provenance and version information for its geographic assets to support factual traceability and reproducible evaluation. City and POI records include data sources, build time, generation method, provider identifiers, and their corresponding world and city versions. GeoWorld adopts a two-level versioning scheme consisting of a global world version and city-level versions, with each city’s assets bound to a specific version. Route caches are treated as derived assets that can be extended as needed during construction and are fixed to a versioned snapshot before evaluation, ensuring that different tasks and repeated runs are based on a consistent geographic substrate.

A.2 Temporal Dynamics and Runtime

GeoWorld represents world changes as events occurring along a unified virtual timeline. Each event describes an external state change, including its occurrence time, the affected place or region, and the corresponding state update. Changes that persist for a period of time additionally record their effective interval, while changes with sequential relationships are linked through event dependencies. These events operate on the fixed geographic substrate, allowing the same place, route, or region to correspond to different service, traffic, weather, or regional states at different times. Complete event definitions are maintained internally by the environment, while the information observable to the Agent consists only of the public states and queryable information produced by events at the current time. At any virtual time, GeoWorld resolves the world state from events that have already occurred and remain effective. For events with causal relationships, a subsequent change enters the world state only after its prerequisite change has occurred. For example, an event defined as the consequence of another change does not appear simply because its scheduled time has been reached. Time therefore determines when a change becomes eligible to occur, while event dependencies ensure that related changes unfold according to their predefined relationships. For changes with a finite duration, their effects are removed from the current state after the effective interval ends, and the resulting state is determined by the underlying state together with other updates that remain effective. A dynamic episode begins from a predefined world state and virtual time. When the Agent wishes to continue the task, it can explicitly advance the virtual clock to a later absolute time. GeoWorld then processes the events that have taken effect during this interval and updates the environment to the world state to the target time. Subsequent queries are executed against that state, as illustrated in Figure 12.

This separates temporal control from environment evolution. The Agent decides when to advance and re-observe the world, whereas the external changes that occur during the interval are determined by GeoWorld’s predefined event schedule. For these exogenous changes, the Agent’s queries and decisions do not alter their order or content. Different Agents can therefore face the same initial state and event schedule while independently deciding when to acquire updated world information. The fixed event schedule also allows the same dynamic process to be replayed across runs, providing controlled conditions for comparing Agent behavior under consistent environmental changes.

A.3 Tool Interfaces and Interaction Protocol

GeoWorld provides agents with a unified interface through 8 public App namespaces and 31 tools. Apps organize different types of world information and operations, while Tools are the concrete interfaces that agents can invoke within the corresponding Apps. The currently available Apps include SystemApp, MapApp, LocalServiceApp, WeatherApp, CityNewsApp, CalendarApp, MessagingApp, and UserInterfaceApp. At the beginning of a run, only the system entry point for opening Apps is typically available. After an agent opens an App, it obtains the tools and corresponding schemas available from that App for the current task. This organization enables tool capabilities to be progressively exposed according to task requirements without modifying the underlying world state. These Apps provide different views of the same runtime environment. Map and routing interfaces expose places, spatial relations, and mobility information; local-service, weather, and city-information interfaces provide current service and environmental conditions; calendar and messaging interfaces provide participant-related information and communication capabilities; and UserInterfaceApp handles plan submission, virtual-time advancement, and task termination. All queries are executed against the world state at the current virtual time. Consequently, invoking the same interface at different times may return different results as the world evolves.

GeoWorld further distinguishes agent operations from exogenous environmental changes. Some tools can update interaction states within the current run, such as sending messages, recording location selections, or submitting plans. advance_simulation advances the virtual clock, after which GeoWorld applies the pre-scheduled events whose temporal conditions have been satisfied. The agent has read-only access to environmental states and cannot directly modify weather, traffic, predefined service states, or the event schedule through the available tools. The agent can therefore decide what information to query, which permitted operations to perform, and when to advance virtual time, while changes in the external environment remain governed by GeoWorld’s event process. GeoWorld records the tool interaction trajectory, including tool names, invocation arguments, returned results, real execution timestamps, and tool execution latency. Model outputs and available token-usage information are also stored during each run. Dynamic episodes additionally maintain virtual-time and event logs, which are used to determine which environmental changes had taken effect when each query was issued. Tool trajectories and temporal event logs are aligned according to execution order. This makes it possible to reconstruct what information the agent queried, what observations it actually received, and which environmental state those observations corresponded to, providing auditable interaction records for subsequent task verification and behavioral analysis.

A.4 World Inspection and Visualization Interface

GeoWorld provides a unified review interface for jointly inspecting tasks, world information, and model execution results, as shown in Figure 13. The review workspace integrates task review, App content inspection, and test results, while the world view provides the spatial and temporal information. The map displays POIs, transportation corridors and routes, task-relevant locations, participant positions, event-affected areas with spatial extents, and task protection areas, allowing reviewers to directly inspect the locations, mobility relations, and spatial constraints involved in a task.

For dynamic tasks, the interface further provides temporal and state information about events. Reviewers can inspect the event type, associated App, affected object or spatial scope, effective time, state update, and causal parents, and can filter events by time range. The event overview also presents their start and end times together with their spatial distribution. This information is used to verify whether the environmental changes relevant to a task are consistent with the corresponding locations, times, and constraints. The interface also supports inspection of saved agent trajectories, including tool calls, arguments, returned results, model inputs and outputs, usage information, and execution latency, allowing task content, world changes, and the information actually obtained by the agent to be examined within the same review workflow.

The interface primarily supports benchmark construction, quality review, and post-hoc analysis. During task construction, reviewers can inspect the relevant locations, routes, events, and constraints, and verify whether the reference answer is consistent with the underlying world information. After experiments, task information and saved tool trajectories can be examined together to analyze the agent’s information acquisition and decision-making process. The review interface is primarily inspection-oriented, while allowing task prompts, reference answers, and constraints to be edited within the permitted scope and review comments to be recorded.

Appendix B LiveGeo: Benchmark Details

B.1 Task Taxonomy

A dependency view of geographic decision-making.

LiveGeo is organized around a simple premise: a geographic decision is valid only insofar as the geographic evidence and constraints on which it depends remain satisfied. We therefore structure the benchmark not by application scenario, but by the dependency structure underlying a decision. The taxonomy progresses from decisions whose validity can be established locally, to decisions whose feasibility depends on several conditions holding jointly, and finally to settings in which those supporting conditions may themselves change over time. In this sense, the three levels of LiveGeo correspond to establishing, composing, and maintaining geographic decision validity.

The static benchmark contains 1,088 instances, including 478 Atomic Geo Tasks and 610 Compositional Geo Tasks. Their distribution is summarized in Table 5. Dynamic Tasks are constructed as matched extensions of applicable static instances and are therefore counted separately.

All candidate instances are independently inspected by three human reviewers before inclusion in the benchmark. Reviewers check the instantiated entities and world state, task constraints, reference solution, supporting evidence, and, for dynamic tasks, the consistency of the event timeline. Inclusion requires unanimous reviewer approval. Table 5 reports the fraction of generated candidates that pass this review process. The consistently high acceptance rates indicate that the construction pipeline produces largely review-ready instances, while human inspection provides a final safeguard against residual factual or specification errors.

Atomic Geo Tasks: establishing local validity.

At the atomic level, LiveGeo isolates three primitives that recur throughout geographic decision-making: resolving what place the available evidence refers to, determining which place satisfies a stated need, and deciding whether movement among places is feasible. We refer to these primitives as Grounding, Discovery, and Mobility Planning, respectively. “Atomic” here describes the structure of the decision rather than the complexity of the trajectory: an instance may require multiple observations, searches, and tool calls, while still centering on a single dominant geographic dependency.

Grounding establishes the correspondence between observations and geographic entities. Street-level evidence rarely identifies the target in isolation: storefronts, road geometry, landmarks, signs, and neighboring places jointly constrain where the scene can be, while the most visually salient object need not be the entity being asked for. The task therefore requires the agent to move from perceptual clues to a geographically verified referent, separating evidence that merely locates the surrounding scene from evidence that identifies the requested place itself. This entity-level correspondence provides the anchor on which later geographic reasoning depends.

Discovery shifts the problem from identifying a given place to choosing one. A user specifies a need and a set of spatial, temporal, or service-related conditions, but leaves the destination unresolved. Candidate retrieval alone does not settle the decision: many places may match the broad activity, while only a subset satisfy the particular conjunction of requirements. Discovery thus tests whether an agent can transform intent into a candidate space and, crucially, use the stated constraints to reduce that space to a defensible geographic choice.

Mobility Planning introduces relations among already identified places. Here, validity is no longer a property of a destination alone, but of a journey through space and time. Waypoints, travel modes, dwell times, visiting order, and deadlines interact cumulatively, so individually feasible route segments need not compose into a feasible trip. The benchmark consequently treats mobility as a constraint-satisfaction problem over the complete journey, including instances in which no arrangement satisfies all requirements. What matters is not recovering a preferred route, but correctly determining whether the requested movement is executable.

11footnotetext: All participant names in LiveGeo tasks are fictional and generated by the GeoWorld simulator.

Together, these three tasks define the local building blocks of LiveGeo: grounding establishes the entities under discussion, discovery chooses among them, and mobility planning determines whether they can be connected through feasible action.

Compositional Geo Tasks: when local validity is not enough.

Real geographic decisions rarely remain isolated. A venue that is suitable for one person may fail for a group; an activity that fits one afternoon may break a three-day itinerary; an otherwise convenient destination may become inappropriate under hazardous weather or regional constraints. Compositional Geo Tasks are designed around precisely this gap between local plausibility and global validity. They retain the geographic primitives above, but introduce an additional dependency whose satisfaction can invalidate an otherwise reasonable local choice.

The four categories differ in where that dependency resides. In Multi-Entity tasks, it lies across participants: locations, travel times, availability windows, and preferences must intersect at a shared activity. The relevant question is therefore not whether each participant can independently reach a venue, but whether their individual feasible sets admit a common solution.

In Long-Horizon tasks, the dependency instead propagates forward through a sequence of activities. Each decision changes the temporal and geographic state from which the next one must be made. A museum, restaurant, or meeting may be perfectly suitable in isolation yet render a later commitment unreachable. The resulting challenge is to preserve feasibility across a chain of decisions, rather than repeatedly optimizing each step in isolation.

Safety-Aware tasks place the additional dependency in the surrounding environment. Geographic suitability is conditional on the state of the world at the relevant place and time: weather, hazards, or other safety-relevant conditions may remove an otherwise valid option from the feasible set. Importantly, LiveGeo does not infer safety awareness merely from the final answer. The interaction trajectory must show that the relevant environmental evidence was acquired, localized to the activity or access route, and allowed to affect the decision.

Finally, Region-Aware tasks introduce dependencies that arise from geographic context. Places that are indistinguishable under generic service or accessibility criteria may cease to be equivalent once local conventions, schedules, practices, or other region-specific conditions are taken into account. The benchmark therefore asks whether regional understanding becomes operational: it must alter which choices remain valid, rather than appearing as contextual knowledge in the explanation.

Viewed together, these categories correspond to four qualitatively different ways in which an apparently valid local decision can fail: because it conflicts with another entity, with a later decision, with the current environment, or with the regional context. This is the central distinction between atomic and compositional evaluation in LiveGeo. The latter is not intended simply to produce longer or more complicated prompts; it tests whether agents can identify and preserve the dependencies that make a collection of local choices jointly executable.

Dynamic Tasks: from decision validity to decision maintenance.

The distinction above still assumes that the evidence supporting a decision remains fixed while the task is being solved. Dynamic Tasks remove this assumption. They are constructed from Mobility Planning and the four compositional categories using matched static–dynamic pairs that share the same objective, initial constraints, and initial world state. What changes is not the task, but the world in which the task continues to unfold.

This design shifts the object of evaluation. In a static task, the central question is whether the agent can establish that a decision is valid under the observed state. In a dynamic task, the question becomes whether the agent can preserve that validity as the supporting state evolves. A traffic disruption may invalidate a timing constraint; a place-state update may eliminate a selected destination; changing weather may alter the safety of an activity; or a participant’s availability may remove the overlap on which a group plan relied. Conversely, many changes may occur without touching any dependency of the current decision.

Reliable behavior therefore requires more than reacting to change. The agent must determine which changes intersect the dependency structure of the current plan, revalidate only the decisions whose support has been affected, and revise them without unnecessarily disturbing constraints that still hold. A change that does not alter the basis of the decision should leave the decision intact; a change that does must propagate to the appropriate downstream choices.

Dynamic LiveGeo thus evaluates selective decision maintenance: the ability to keep a geographic decision aligned with the evidence that justifies it as the world evolves. In combination with the static taxonomy, this yields the full progression studied by the benchmark—from establishing individual geographic relations, to composing them into executable decisions, to maintaining those decisions when their supporting conditions no longer remain fixed.

B.2 Task Construction Details

LiveGeo constructs geographic tasks through a capability-driven task construction workflow grounded in GeoWorld. GeoWorld provides the geographic entities, attributes, routes, and world states needed to define and verify task requirements, while task-specific construction logic determines how these resources are used to instantiate different geographic capabilities. By separating the underlying world from task construction, the same environment can support new task types without requiring changes to its geographic infrastructure.

B.2.1 GT Selection

Static GT selection.

All LiveGeo tasks are constructed from a fixed version of GeoWorld, which provides real-world POIs, their attributes, route information, and other geographic facts. Based on these facts, we determine the ground truth (GT) for each task through task-specific procedures. For Grounding, Discovery, Multi-Entity, Safety-Aware, and Region-Aware tasks, GT is selected programmatically from real POIs according to the requirements of each task category. For Long-Horizon tasks, an LLM suggests the types of activities to include, while code selects the corresponding real POIs to form an ordered sequence as GT. Mobility Planning follows a different procedure: code first selects the locations and constructs travel constraints, and a solver then determines whether the trip is feasible, producing a Boolean GT.

Importantly, selecting a GT does not mean that it is already a verified answer. For POI-based tasks, the selected GT serves as the starting point for constructing constraints C0C_{0} using facts from GeoWorld. We then verify whether GT constitutes a feasible solution under the constructed constraints and whether these constraints are supported by world facts. Only tasks that pass the subsequent verification procedures are retained in LiveGeo. Table 6 summarizes the GT selection procedures across task categories, together with illustrative examples.

Dynamic GT selection.

For dynamic tasks, we start from a verified static task with its initial GT G​T0GT_{0}. Before constructing dynamic events, we select a later GT G​T1GT_{1} that the events are intended to make valid. For POI-based tasks, an LLM may suggest the direction of change, while code selects G​T1GT_{1} from real POIs in GeoWorld. For example, in a Multi-Entity task in London, the initial GT is Bonne Bouche Paddington (G​T0GT_{0}), while the later GT is Hayat Paddington (G​T1GT_{1}). A temporary closure of the original venue is then introduced as an event, and subsequent verification checks whether the updated world state supports G​T1GT_{1}. As with static tasks, the selected GT becomes a verified reference answer only after the corresponding construction and verification procedures.

B.2.2 Constraint and Task Construction

Static constraint and task construction.

We construct task constraints C0C_{0} by translating relevant facts in GeoWorld into explicit user requirements. World facts describe actual conditions, such as opening hours and travel times, while constraints specify what a valid solution must satisfy, such as being open from 18:00 to 19:00 or reachable within 20 minutes. Not every available fact becomes a constraint. For POI-based tasks, we establish a candidate set, derive possible constraints from their attributes and route information, and examine how individual constraints and their combinations affect the GT and other candidates. The selected constraints are recorded with their values, units, and supporting facts for subsequent verification.

The construction procedure depends on what each task is designed to evaluate. For Grounding, we first select a target POI and collect multi-directional images from Google Street View22 2 https://www.google.com/streetview/. As illustrated in Figure 14, an LLM writer uses these images, geographic attributes, and nearby landmarks to generate a natural-language identification request. Visual clues are drawn from the evaluation image, while information from other views is incorporated into the request as textual clues. The writer records the supporting evidence for each clue. The generated task undergoes automated checks for image validity, spatial correspondence, and answer leakage, followed by human review of its factual and visual consistency.

For Discovery, the goal is to construct constraints that distinguish the GT from nearby candidates. We first select a character with a public starting location and fix a target POI (GT). The GT’s place type defines the base constraint C0C_{0}, which is retained in all subsequent constraint combinations. As illustrated in Figure 15, we then construct a local candidate pool of nearby POIs matching C0C_{0} and collect their geographic attributes and routing information from the character’s starting location. Code generates fact-supported additional constraints, evaluates them against the candidates, and searches for combinations with the fewest additional constraints that distinguish the GT within this pool. The LLM writer selects one verified option and expresses all its conditions in a natural-language request without modifying them. The generated task undergoes automated checks and human review before inclusion in LiveGeo.

For Mobility Planning, we first sample an origin, a destination, and optional waypoints with a fixed visit order and required activities. We then retrieve real routes for each trip leg across different travel modes and enumerate complete trip plans. Based on these plans, we construct travel constraints, including time limits, prohibited travel modes, walking distance limits, and required stop durations, and compute the feasibility ground truth (GT) by checking whether any complete plan satisfies all constraints. Finally, an LLM writer converts the fixed trip specification and constraints into a natural-language request, followed by automatic validation and human review. The construction process is illustrated in Figure 16.

For Multi-Entity, constraints must account for both individual requirements and the feasibility of a shared activity. We first select participants, a target POI, and comparison candidates from GeoWorld. Using real travel routes and participant availability, we construct the initial constraints C0C_{0} and verify the feasibility of the shared activity. An LLM then adds fact-supported constraints Δ​C\Delta C to distinguish the fixed GT from other feasible candidates and generates a corresponding natural-language request. The construction process is illustrated in Figure 17.

For Long-Horizon, a feasible multi-day reference itinerary is constructed by iteratively filling the time windows between fixed commitments. At each step, activities are selected, real POIs are sampled when needed, and route and time feasibility are checked before new nodes are appended to the timeline.The completed itinerary is then used to derive constraints for each POI activity, as illustrated in Figure 18. Constraints operate at two levels: individual activities must satisfy their location, service, and time requirements, while the full itinerary must respect activity order, travel times, durations, and fixed commitments such as hotel check-in and departure. Importantly, detailed schedules stored in the reference itinerary serve as feasibility evidence and are not automatically included as user constraints.

Safety-Aware follow a different construction principle: ordinary constraints C0C_{0} must not independently determine the GT. For Safety-Aware tasks, C0C_{0} is constructed to retain both the GT and at least one competing location, so that an additional safety condition EE is necessary to distinguish the safe choice. For example, two hotels may satisfy the same travel and availability requirements, but only one remains suitable under the given safety conditions. This ensures that identifying the correct location requires considering current safety information rather than relying on ordinary place constraints alone. The construction process is illustrated in Figure 19.

For Region-Aware tasks, regional criteria RR are derived from Wikivoyage33 3 https://en.wikivoyage.org/. We use GPT-5.6 Sol to extract region-specific constraints from Wikivoyage pages, select those that can affect POI selection, and verify them through human review. The GT must satisfy both the ordinary constraints C0C_{0} and the regional criterion RR. We construct C0C_{0} to exclude other candidates satisfying RR, while retaining at least one candidate that satisfies C0C_{0} but not RR. This ensures that the regional criterion is necessary to identify the GT, rather than being an optional detail that does not affect the decision. The construction process is illustrated in Figure 20.

Dynamic constraint and task construction.

Dynamic tasks are constructed from verified static tasks, inheriting the user request, initial constraints C0C_{0}, ground truth G​T0GT_{0}, and world state W0W_{0}. A Direction Agent first identifies the dimensions along which the target outcome should change, based on the original task and available geographic facts. For place-selection tasks, these dimensions guide the filtering of a local candidate pool, from which a new target G​T1GT_{1} is sampled and fixed before event generation. When changes to the task requirements are needed, target constraints C1C_{1} are constructed using the facts of G​T1GT_{1} and comparisons with eligible candidates, while unaffected requirements from C0C_{0} are preserved.

In the example shown in Figure 21, the target constraints retain G​T1GT_{1} and two competing POIs before the events are applied. These target constraints guide event construction. Given the fixed G​T1GT_{1}, the target constraint changes, and relevant world information, a construction LLM, referred to as the Event Author, generates a complete sequence of timestamped events. Each event contains a public message, observable through the corresponding application, and a structured update specifying its effects on the world. The number and types of events depend on the task. In Figure 21, the first event updates the user’s activity and regional requirements, while the subsequent events temporarily close one competing POI and disrupt travel to another. Together, these events allow the fixed G​T1GT_{1} to become the unique feasible choice. Events may also involve weather, participant availability, or other changes to the environment. The Event Author cannot alter the fixed G​T1GT_{1} or the underlying geographic facts. Each event records its publication time, effective interval, affected entities, and supporting references, allowing announcements and their actual effects to be distinguished.

The generated events are replayed chronologically in a temporary world state. Both user messages and environmental changes update the evolving world, while the effective task constraints reflect any explicit changes to user or participant requirements. Verification checks the validity of event references, temporal consistency, the feasibility of the resulting state changes, and whether the final outcome matches the fixed G​T1GT_{1}. For place-selection tasks, this includes checking the remaining candidates against the effective constraints and updated world state. Human reviewers further assess the plausibility of the events and the consistency between public messages and structured updates. Only validated event sequences that do not conflict with existing events or protected task dependencies are incorporated into the shared world timeline.

Notably, for Mobility Planning, the ground truth is a Boolean feasibility judgment. We sample whether G​T1GT_{1} preserves or reverses G​T0GT_{0} with equal probability, then generate events to realize the target outcome under the effective travel requirements and route conditions. For example, a traffic disruption may cause a previously feasible journey to exceed its travel-time limit, making it infeasible, whereas a less severe delay may leave its feasibility unchanged. After event replay, we recompute journey feasibility to verify G​T1GT_{1}.

Event protection.

As dynamic tasks are progressively constructed and incorporated into the shared world timeline, newly generated events may conflict with existing events in space and time or affect the world states on which the ground truths of previous tasks depend. To prevent interference between tasks while allowing diverse events to coexist in the same geographic world, we introduce an event protection mechanism. This mechanism maintains two types of historical records: (1) the affected geographic scopes and effective intervals of committed events, and (2) the resources on which the ground truths of previously validated tasks depend, including places, routes, usage times, and participant or user request identities.

As illustrated in Figure 22, before generating new dynamic events, we define a local spatiotemporal scope based on the places, routes, and time window relevant to the current task. We then retrieve historical event footprints and protected task dependencies relevant to this scope. Both types of records are filtered based on spatial intersection and temporal relevance, and the results are visualized using distinct colors and markers on a private map provided to the Event Author. The map displays the affected areas of existing events alongside protected places and routes, allowing the Event Author to identify potential spatiotemporal conflicts and select appropriate event locations and times. Participant and user request identity dependencies are not visualized on the map but are checked separately during subsequent verification.

After event generation, we determine the actual affected scopes and effective intervals from the structured updates and check them against the complete historical records. For geographically relevant records, a spatiotemporal conflict occurs only when a new event spatially intersects a historical protection record and their effective intervals overlap. Spatial intersections are determined using the original geographic geometries, including boundary contact. Temporal overlap is determined using half-open intervals: two intervals [s1,e1)[s_{1},e_{1}) and [s2,e2)[s_{2},e_{2}) overlap if s1<e2s_{1}<e_{2} and s2<e1s_{2}<e_{1}. For identity-related records, we further check whether a new event affects the same participant or user request during an overlapping time interval. When a conflict is detected, the relevant records and reasons for the conflict are returned to the Event Author to revise the event sequence, followed by another round of verification.

Only events that pass the complete historical conflict checks are committed to the shared world timeline. Their corresponding event records and task protection information are also retained for subsequent tasks. Notably, overlapping protection scopes do not inherently constitute a conflict. For example, two tasks may depend on the same route or use the same place at different times. The mechanism restricts new events that conflict with existing protection records, rather than preventing tasks from sharing geographic resources. In this way, GeoWorld preserves the validity of historical tasks and supports the continued accumulation of dynamic events within the same geographic environment without requiring tasks to occupy entirely separate spatial or temporal regions.

B.2.3 Task Verification

Static task verification.

We verify each constructed task through programmatic checks before generating the final user request. The verification covers three main aspects. (1) Fact Support: All entities, place attributes, and route information used in the task must be supported by records from the corresponding GeoWorld version. Missing information is not treated as a negative fact; for example, an unavailable route record cannot be used to conclude that a destination is unreachable. (2) Constraint Consistency: Each constraint must specify its applicable entity, condition, value, unit, and relevant temporal or spatial context. We check that the constraints are well-defined, mutually consistent, and supported by the available facts. (3) GT Validity: We determine whether the GT constitutes a valid solution under the complete task requirements and whether the required distinctions between candidates hold. Since different task categories have different validity conditions, we apply task-specific verification rules, summarized in Table 7. Here, EE denotes the safety-related environmental conditions in Safety-Aware tasks, while RR denotes the region-specific criteria in Region-Aware tasks.

Beyond these checks, we verify Public Observability, ensuring that the information needed to solve the task can be obtained through the user request or available agent tools, rather than relying on hidden construction records. This does not require exposing internal GT labels or region-specific criteria directly to the agent; instead, the available geographic facts and task context must provide sufficient information for the intended decision.

After programmatic verification, the LLM writer converts the structured task into a natural-language request. We check whether the generated request preserves all selected constraints without changing their values, omitting requirements, introducing unsupported conditions, or revealing the GT. Human reviewers further examine the request, supporting evidence, and potential ambiguities that programmatic checks may not fully capture. Tasks that fail these checks are revised or discarded according to the corresponding construction rules.

Dynamic task verification.

Dynamic verification extends the static procedure to changes in world states and task requirements. We first check that the dynamic task preserves the initial world state, user request, constraints C0C_{0}, and GT G​T0GT_{0} of its static counterpart. We then verify the generated events, checking that their affected entities, timestamps, observable messages, and corresponding state updates are valid and consistent.

Next, we apply the events in chronological order to reconstruct the evolving world states and effective task constraints. Environmental changes update the corresponding world states, while explicit changes to user or participant requirements update the affected constraints without altering the remaining requirements. Based on these updated conditions, we verify whether the predefined G​T1GT_{1} becomes a valid solution and whether the intended change from G​T0GT_{0} to G​T1GT_{1} is supported by the resulting world state. For example, when Restaurant A closes and Restaurant B extends its opening hours, we check that these events produce the corresponding state updates and that B becomes a valid choice under the original dining requirements.

We also verify that each event has a valid and observable effect, although an individual event need not independently change the final GT. When events are integrated into a shared world timeline, additional checks ensure that they do not conflict with existing events or invalidate protected task dependencies. Finally, human reviewers examine the event sequence, its effects on the task, and the supporting evidence. Only tasks that pass the required programmatic checks and human review are retained in LiveGeo.

B.3 Evaluation Details

This section details the evaluation indicators and correctness criteria for each LiveGeo task category. Beyond determining overall task success, we use these indicators to further analyze model performance and failure patterns across task categories in Appendix C.3.

B.3.1 Grounding

We evaluate grounding at two complementary levels: whether the agent selects the correct geographic entity through tool interaction, and whether it communicates the correct grounded result in its final response. This distinction mirrors everyday wayfinding: when helping someone locate a place, one must not only identify the correct location, but also communicate it clearly to the person asking. Accordingly, we define two indicators, Tool-grounded and User-facing, as summarized in Table 8. Together, they capture the two stages of grounding: selecting the correct location in the environment and communicating that result to the user.

Overall grounding correctness.

A test instance is considered correctly grounded only when both indicators pass. Formally, let TT denote the Tool-grounded indicator and UU denote the User-facing indicator. We define the overall grounding outcome as

G=T∧U.G=T\land U.
